translations.text: "Jesus, walking by the Sea of Galilee," and so on.
Once Christ was walking by the Sea of Galilee, and he saw two brothers: Simon, who was called Peter, and his brother Andrew, and so on.
Just as they had earlier fished with a net in the waves of the sea, so Christ made them afterwards fish for men's souls with his heavenly teaching;

because they drew people away from fleshly lusts and from worldly errors to the stability of the land of the living, that is, to the eternal homeland, about which the prophet said through God's Spirit,
"I will send my fishers, and they will fish for them; my hunters, and they will hunt them from every mountain and from every hill."

The Lord chose fishermen and unlearned men as his disciples, and taught them so well that their teaching surpassed all the wisdom of the world, and by their preaching they turned emperors and kings to the true faith.

If the Saviour had chosen eloquent teachers and worldly philosophers at the beginning and sent such men out to preach, then it would have seemed as if the true faith had not sprung up through God's might, but from worldly eloquence.
He chose fishermen before he chose emperors, because it is better that the emperor, when he comes to Rome,
should cast off his crown and kneel at the fisherman's shrine than that the fisherman should kneel at the emperor's shrine.
He did choose emperors, but he still ranked the poor fisherman before the powerful emperor.
Afterwards he chose the wealthy. But if he had not first chosen the poor, it would have seemed to the wealthy that they had been chosen for their possessions.
Later he chose worldly philosophers, but they would have grown proud if he had not first chosen the unlearned fishermen.
Consider now how the Lord took glory away from mankind so that he might give them glory. He took our vain glory from us so that he might give us the eternal glory.
You must not glory in yourself, but, as the apostle said, "He who glories, let him glory in God."
At Christ's command, Peter and Andrew immediately left their nets and followed him.

They had not yet seen him work any miracles, nor had they yet heard anything from his mouth about the reward of the eternal recompense, and yet, at the sound of a single command, they forgot what they had.

We have heard and also seen many of God's miracles; we are often afflicted with many scourges and terrified by the harshness of many threats, and yet we despise God's command and will not follow him on the way of life.
Now he sits in heaven, clothed in the human nature that he took on in this life. He urges us to turn to him, so that we always cleanse our ways of sins and correct them according to his commandments.

He has completely bowed the necks of the nations under his yoke; he has cast down the glory of the world, and by repeated downfalls he shows that his strict judgment is approaching; and yet our proud mind will not give up of its own will what it loses daily by compulsion.
My brothers, what plea can we make at his judgment, since we will not turn away from this present love of the world in obedience to his commandments, and we are not corrected by his scourges?
Perhaps one of you says to himself in silent thought: "What did these brothers, Peter and Andrew, give up, when they had almost nothing?"
But in this matter we should consider their desire more than their wealth. Whoever keeps nothing for himself gives up a great deal.
Truly, we hold on to our possessions with great love, and the things we do not have we seek with immense desire.
Peter and Andrew gave up a great deal when each of them completely gave up the wish to own things and renounced his own desires.
Now someone says, "I would like to imitate the apostles, who scorned all worldly things, but I have no possessions to give up."
But God looks at a man's heart and not at his possessions. He does not count how much wealth we spend on offerings to him; rather, he looks at how much desire we have when we offer him those gifts.
See: these holy merchants, Peter and Andrew, bought eternal life for themselves with their nets and their boat.
The kingdom of God has no fixed price. It is valued according to what a person has.

The kingdom of heaven was given to these brothers we have mentioned in return for their net and boat. Later it was given to the rich man Zacchaeus for half of his possessions, to a certain widow for a farthing, and to a certain man for a drink of water.
I think these words will not be fully clear to you unless we explain them to you more openly.
"Zacchaeus was a rich man, and he watched for the Saviour's coming and wanted to see who he was; but he could not because of the crowd that went with him, for he was short in stature.
Then he ran ahead of the Saviour and climbed up into a tree, so that he might see him.
Then Christ looked up at the rich man and said, "Zacchaeus, come down quickly, because today I must stay at your house."
Zacchaeus then swiftly came down from the tree and received him rejoicing." When Zacchaeus had invited Christ, he stood before him and said to him resolutely,
"Lord, behold, I give half of my goods to the poor, and whatever I have taken by fraud, I will repay fourfold."
The Lord said to him, "Now today salvation has come to this household, because he is a descendant of Abraham.
I have come to seek and to save what was lost among mankind." So Zacchaeus had bought the kingdom of heaven with half of his possessions;
the other half he kept so that he could repay fourfold those whom he had wrongfully robbed before.
Again: "On one occasion the Saviour sat in the temple at Jerusalem, in front of the treasury, and watched how the people threw their alms into the treasury, and many rich people brought great gifts.
Then a poor widow came there and offered a farthing to God.
Then the Lord said to his disciples, "I tell you truly, this poor widow has brought a greater offering than any of these rich men."
They all gave whatever portion of their wealth seemed right to them, but this widow offered all her living with a devout mind."
So the poor widow had bought eternal life with a little money, that is, with a single farthing.
In one place the Saviour said to his apostles, "Truly I tell you, whoever gives cold water to drink to one thirsty man among those who believe in me, his reward will not be lost."
My brothers, consider now at how cheap a price the kingdom of God is bought, and how precious it is to possess.
The price cannot be raised by any payment, but it is offered to each person according to his own means.
We read about Christ's birth that heavenly angels were seen above the newborn child, and they sang this hymn of praise with great joy,
"Gloria in excelsis Deo, et in terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis": that is, in our language,
"Glory be to God in the highest, and on earth peace to the men who are of good will." No offering is as pleasing to God as good will.
If anyone does not have the means to offer visible gifts to God, let him offer the invisible one, that is, good will, which incomparably surpasses earthly riches.
What is good will but goodness: that a person grieves at another man's misfortune and rejoices in his prosperity, and loves his friend not for worldly reasons but for God's sake;
that he bears with his enemy in love, commands no one to do what would not please himself, helps his neighbour's need as far as he is able, and beyond his ability, with his will?
What is any offering compared with this will, when the soul offers itself to God on the altar of its heart? About this the psalmist said,
"In me sunt, Deus, vota tua, quae reddam laudationes tibi": "Almighty God, your vows are upon me, which I will repay to you with praises."
As if he were saying openly: Though I do not have outward gifts to offer you, I nevertheless find in myself something that I may lay on the altar of your praise;
For you do not live on our gifts. Instead, you are more delighted by the offering of our heart.
This offering cannot be in a heart that is occupied with greed or envy, for these are opposed to good will, and as soon as they touch the mind, good will departs:
For this reason the holy preachers would not covet anything in this world with greed, nor have any private possessions, so that they could love one another deeply, without envy.
Truly, the prophet Isaiah foresaw these apostles who were to come, when he said through God's Spirit,
"Who are these who fly here like clouds, and like doves to their windows?"
The prophet saw them despise earthly possessions, draw near to heaven with their minds, abound in the words of life and shine with miracles, and he called them doves and flying clouds.
Our windows are our eyes, through which our soul looks at whatever it desires outside. The dove is a gentle creature, free from the bitterness of gall.
Truly the holy apostles were like doves at their windows, since they desired nothing in this world,
but looked upon all things innocently, and were not drawn by any eagerness for plunder toward what they saw outside.
He who desires through plunder the things that he sees outside with his eyes is a kite, not a dove at his windows.
We have now gone through part of the commentary on this gospel. Now we will tell you the meaning of the names of the four apostles whom Christ chose at the beginning.

Simon is interpreted as 'obedient,' and Peter as 'acknowledging,' Andrew as 'manly'; James is called 'supplanter,' and John 'God's grace.' Every Christian should keep the meaning of these names fully in his way of life.
Peter was called Simon before his conversion, but Christ named him Peter, which means 'acknowledging', because he acknowledged Christ with true faith when he said,
"You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Without doubt, whoever rightly acknowledges God and obeys him holds in his way of life the meaning of these two names.
If he bears hardship manfully for God's name, and resists the devil's temptations like a man, then he fulfils in his conduct the meaning of Andrew, which is interpreted as 'manly.'
James is called 'supplanter,' and he is a true supplanter who wisely supplants his fleshly sins and the devil's enticement.
John is called 'God's grace.' He is fittingly called God's grace who through good merits obtains God's grace, so that he may zealously fulfil his commandments.
After Christ's passion, the apostle Andrew went to the land called Achaia. There he preached faith in the Lord and the redemption of the world through his passion.
Then Aegeas, a cruel judge, wanted to stamp out his preaching and force the Christians into devilish worship. Andrew said to him,
"Since you are a judge of men, it would be fitting for you to acknowledge your Judge, who is in heaven, and to worship him who is the true God, and to turn your mind away from the false gods."
Aegeas answered him, "Are you Andrew, who overthrows the temples of our gods and incites this people to the vain teaching that the Roman rulers have rejected and ordered to be stamped out?"
Andrew answered him, "The Roman rulers have not yet acknowledged God's truth: how the Son of God came to men and taught that these idols
that you worship are not gods at all, but are the worst devils, enemies of mankind, who teach men how to anger Almighty God,
"And then he abandons them, and the devil mocks them until they leave their bodies guilty and naked, taking nothing with them except their sins."
Aegeas said, "These are idle words. Indeed, when your Saviour preached these words, the Jews fastened him to the gallows of the cross." Andrew answered him,

"Oh, if only you were willing to know the mystery of the holy cross: with what reasonable love the Lord of mankind accepted the gallows of the cross for our restoration, not by compulsion, but of his own will."
Aegeas said, "How can you say of his own will, when he was betrayed, and hanged by the governor's soldiers at the request of the Jews?" Andrew answered,
"I said of his own will because I was with him when he was betrayed by his disciple, and before his passion he told us beforehand,
and that he would rise from death on the third day. He said that he had power to give up his soul, and power to take it back again." Aegeas said,
"I am surprised that you, a wise man, want to follow this teaching, however it came about, willingly or by compulsion, that he was fastened on the cross."
Andrew answered him, "Great is the mystery of the cross, which I will reveal to you, if you are willing to hear me." Egeas said, "It cannot truly be called a mystery, but a punishment."
Andrew said, "You will understand that this very punishment is the mystery of mankind's renewal, if you are willing to hear me patiently." Aegeas answered,
"I will hear you patiently, but if you do not obey me, you shall receive the same mystery of the cross on yourself."
Andrew answered him, "If I feared the gallows of the cross, I would not preach the glory of the cross." Aegeas said,
"Your senseless speech proclaims the torment of the cross as glory, because in your presumption you do not fear the torment of death." Andrew answered,
"Not through presumption but through faith I do not fear the torment of death. The death of righteous men is precious, and the death of sinful men is wretched."
Egeas said, "Unless you offer sacrifice to our almighty gods, I will order you to be tormented and fastened on the same cross that you praise."
Andrew said to him, "Every day I offer my sacrifice to Almighty God, who alone is the true God.

Not the flesh of lowing bulls or the blood of goats, but every day I offer on the altar of the holy cross the spotless Lamb, and it remains whole and alive after all the people eat its flesh and drink its blood."
Aegeas asked, "How can that happen?" Andrew answered him,
"If you want to learn how that can happen, then take on the form of a disciple, so that you may learn these mysteries."
Aegeas said, "I will get the understanding of this thing out of you with torments." The holy apostle answered,
"I am greatly amazed at you, that you have turned to such great foolishness as to expect that I would reveal the divine mysteries to you because of torments.
You have heard the mystery of the holy offering. Now, if you believe that Christ, the Son of God, who was hanged on the cross, is true God,
then I will reveal to you how the Lamb remains whole and unblemished in his kingdom after it is offered, and its flesh eaten, and its blood drunk.
But if you will not believe, you will never come to insight into this truth."
So then Egeas grew angry, and ordered the apostle to be thrust into a dark prison.
Then a great crowd from the whole province came to the prison. They wanted to kill Aegeas and lead the apostle out of the prison.
Then Andrew said to all the multitude, "My brothers, do not stir the gentle Lord to any anger by what you are attempting.
Our Saviour was betrayed, and he was patient: he did not quarrel or cry out, nor did anyone hear his voice in the streets.

Keep quiet and peace now, and do not hinder my martyrdom, but rather prepare yourselves as God's soldiers, so that with fearless minds you may overcome all threats and bodily torments through patience.
If any terror is to be feared, then it is the one that has no end. Truly, the fear of man is like smoke, which vanishes quickly when it is stirred.
The pains in this world are either light and bearable, or they are heavy and quickly drive the soul out.

The pains that are prepared for the wicked in the world to come are eternal. There is weeping every day, and wailing, and lamentation, and endless torment, and Egeas is hastening there without hesitation."
Be all the more ready for this, so that through passing affliction you may come to the eternal joys, where you will always rejoice, flourishing and reigning with Christ."
When the apostle had taught the people such words all through the night, at dawn Egeas sent to the prison and ordered the holy apostle to be brought to him, and said,
"I thought that in your reflection during the night you would turn your mind away from folly and stop praising your Christ, so that you might enjoy the pleasures of life with us.
It is foolish for a man to hurry of his own will to the gallows of the cross and send himself to torments." Andrew answered,
"I can have joy with you if you believe in Christ and give up your idols. Christ sent me to this province, where I have won for him no small number of people." Aegeas said,
"That is why I am forcing you to offer to our gods: so that this people whom you deceived may give up the vanity of your teaching, and so that they may offer an acceptable sacrifice to our gods.

There is no city left in all this land in which the temples of our gods have not been abandoned. Now the worship of our gods must be restored again through you, so that they may be gladdened by you and you may be in our friendship.
If you will not do this, then for the protection of our gods you shall suffer various torments, and afterwards perish hanging on the gallows of the cross that you have praised."
The apostle answered him, "You child of death, hear me; you chaff, made ready for eternal burnings, hear me, the servant of God and apostle of the Saviour Christ.
Until now I have spoken to you gently, so that you might acknowledge the true faith through reason. But now you persist in your shamelessness and think that I ought to be afraid of your threats.
Devise whatever more torments seem good to you. The longer I persevere in torments, confessing his name, the more acceptable I shall be to my King."
Then the cruel executioner ordered him to be stretched out and scourged seven times. Afterwards he ordered him to be raised up, and said to him,
"Andrew, listen to me, and change your mind, so that your blood is not shed. If you do not, I will make you perish on the gallows of the cross."
The apostle answered, "I am Christ's servant, and I ought to desire the victory of his cross rather than fear it.
Truly, you can escape the eternal torments that are destined for you if you believe in Christ, now that you have tested my steadfastness.
I fear your damnation, and I am not troubled by my own suffering.
My suffering will end in one day, or two, or at most three; but your torment cannot come to an end within a thousand years.
Therefore, wretched man, do not add any more to your miseries, and do not kindle the eternal fire for yourself."
Then Egeas, enraged, ordered him to be hung on the gallows of the cross. He commanded the executioners to bind him to the cross hand and foot with cords, so that he would suffer for a long time.
Then the Christian people ran toward the executioners who were leading him to the cross, crying out and saying,
"What has this righteous man and friend of God done that he should deserve to hang on a cross?" But Andrew asked the people not to hinder his passion.
He went on with a glad heart, rejoicing and teaching the people. Then he saw from a distance the cross that had been prepared for him, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying,
"Hail, O cross, you who were made holy by Christ's body and adorned with his limbs as if with pearls.
You inspired earthly dread before our Lord mounted you; now you possess heavenly love, and you are ascended for a promise.
Free from care and rejoicing, I come to you, so that you may receive me with rejoicing, the disciple of him who hung on you; for I have always loved you and longed to embrace you.
O good cross, you that received beauty and loveliness from the Lord's limbs, you were long desired and earnestly loved, sought without ceasing, and now at last made ready for my longing mind.
Take me from among men and give me back to my Master, so that he who redeemed me through you may receive me through you."
After these words he took off his clothes and handed his garments over to the executioners.
Then they came up, raised him onto the cross, and bound his whole body with stiff cords, just as they had been commanded.
More than twenty thousand people stood there with Egeas's brother, crying out together, "It is an unjust judgement that this holy man should suffer like this."

Truly, from the cross the holy Andrew strengthened the hearts of the faithful people, urging them to patience in this passing life and saying that this short suffering is not to be compared with the eternal reward.
Meanwhile all the people went to Egeas's residence, all crying out together and saying that so holy a man should not hang there;
a virtuous man, adorned with good conduct, a noble teacher, merciful and kind, wise and pure, ought not to suffer like this, but ought to be released from the cross while still alive;
for he does not stop preaching the truth, though he has now hung there alive for two days.
So Egeas feared the crowd, promised that he would release him as they wished, and went along with them.
When the apostle saw him, he asked, "Well now, Egeas, why have you come to us?
If you are still willing to believe in the Saviour, you will be shown mercy, as I promised you.
If you have come in order to release me, I do not wish to be released from here alive. Now I clearly see my true King; I stand in his sight, praying to him.
I pity you and your misery, for eternal damnation awaits you.
Hurry now, wretched man, while you are still able to do anything, so that you do not end up wanting to when it is denied you."
Then they tried to release him, but the hands of anyone who touched the cross grew stiff.
Then the apostle cried out to the Saviour Christ in a very loud voice, praying like this: "My good Master, do not let me be released unless you first receive my spirit."
After these words a great light was seen coming suddenly from heaven to the apostle. It shone all around him, so that human eyes could not see him because of the heavenly light that surrounded him.
The light remained for nearly an hour, and Andrew gave up his spirit in that light and went to Christ together with the radiance. To Christ be glory for ever throughout all the world.
On the way home, before he reached his house, Egeas was seized by a horrible devil. He went utterly mad and was thrown to the ground in the sight of the people who were walking with him.
So the cruel man departed from the world to hell. His brother kept the body of the holy Andrew with great reverence, so that he might escape [Egeas's fate].
Such great fear spread over all the people that no one was left there who did not believe in God.
The priests and deacons of that people, who saw it all, wrote down this passion, so that no one would doubt this account.
Let us now pray to the Almighty Ruler that his blessed apostle may be our intercessor, just as he was the herald of his Church.
To the Creator Lord be honour and praise for ever and ever. Amen, we say.
